gbs333-aaa394-d1e107.summary: States the question: whether it is possible for the intellect of a wayfarer (viator) to have evident knowledge of theological truths.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e127.summary: Outlines Ockham's procedure in four articles: defining the terms; asking what kind of knowledge of God a created intellect can have; answering the question; and raising and solving doubts.
claims: The question proceeds by defining terms, examining knowledge of God, answering, and resolving doubts.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e144.summary: Announces the three terms to be defined in the first article: the wayfarer's intellect, evident knowledge, and theological truth.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e153.summary: Defines the wayfarer: one not yet at the terminus toward which he tends, the two termini of a rational creature being final beatitude and final misery, so a wayfarer is neither blessed nor finally damned. Since Ockham supposes intuitive knowledge of God beatifies, the definition concerns the pure wayfarer, excluding Christ, who was simultaneously wayfarer and comprehensor with intuitive vision from the instant of his soul's creation. On Paul's rapture (in which, per Augustine to Paulinus, he saw God's essence): either Paul was truly blessed in that instant though not permanently, or, if perpetuity belongs to beatitude, he remained a wayfarer, so that 'permanently' must be added: a wayfarer is one who lacks intuitive knowledge of the deity permanently possible to him by God's ordained power. This excludes the blessed and the damned (for whom such vision is impossible by ordained, though not absolute, power), and shows that Pierre d'Ailly wrongly criticizes Ockham's definition.
claims: A wayfarer is one who is neither finally blessed nor finally damned.
Intuitive knowledge of God is beatifying.
Christ was at once wayfarer and comprehensor, having intuitive vision from the first instant of his soul.
Paul in rapture was either momentarily blessed or remained a wayfarer, depending on whether perpetuity belongs to beatitude.
A wayfarer lacks intuitive knowledge of God permanently possible to him by God's ordained power.
Pierre d'Ailly's criticism of Ockham's definition of the wayfarer is mistaken.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e257.summary: Notes that the comprehensor is known by opposition to the wayfarer.
claims: The comprehensor is defined by opposition to the wayfarer.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e266.summary: Second term, evident knowledge: evidence and inevidence are differences of propositional truth, so incomplex knowledge, being neither true nor false, is neither evident nor inevident. Evidence belongs first to adhesive knowledge (assent) and derivatively to apprehensive knowledge of propositions; a proposition is called evident because assent to it is evident, otherwise every necessary truth would be evident, whereas many are doubtful to us. Ockham defines evident knowledge as adhesive knowledge of a true complex apt to be sufficiently caused, mediately or immediately, by incomplex knowledge of its terms or of another proposition ('immediately' for self-evident or contingent propositions, 'mediately' for demonstrable conclusions). 'Apt to be caused' rather than 'caused' allows that if God directly caused knowledge acquirable by demonstration it would still be evident. Refers to Pierre d'Ailly for fuller treatment.
claims: Evidence and inevidence belong to propositional knowledge, not incomplex knowledge.
Evidence belongs primarily to assent and derivatively to the proposition.
Many necessary propositions are not evident to us.
Evident knowledge is assent to a true complex apt to be sufficiently caused by knowledge of its terms or of other propositions.
Knowledge directly caused by God would still be evident if it is of the kind apt to be caused naturally.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e347.summary: Evident and necessary knowledge are related as impertinent (cross-cutting) terms: not every necessary truth is evident, and not every evident truth is necessary, as with contingent truths known by experience.
claims: Evidence and necessity are independent: some necessary truths are not evident, and some evident truths are contingent.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e373.summary: Evident knowledge is broader than science, understanding, prudence, or any habit listed in Ethics VI, since those concern only necessary truths, while evident knowledge also extends to contingent truths.
claims: Evident knowledge extends more widely than science and the other Aristotelian intellectual habits, covering contingent truths.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e390.summary: Evident proposition is superior to both scientific knowledge and self-evident proposition: every science is evident knowledge and every self-evident proposition is evident, but not conversely, as a contingent truth known by experience is evident yet neither science nor self-evident.
claims: Evident knowledge is a genus above scientific knowledge and self-evident propositions.
Experiential contingent knowledge is evident but neither scientific nor per se nota.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e412.summary: Objection: it follows that an evident contingent proposition would always be self-evident, since knowledge of its terms suffices to cause assent. Ockham replies that self-evidence requires evident knowledge from any knowledge of the terms, whereas a contingent proposition is known only from intuitive, not abstractive, knowledge of its terms.
claims: (Objection) Evident contingent propositions would be self-evident.
A self-evident proposition must be evident from any knowledge of its terms.
Contingent propositions are evident only from intuitive knowledge of their terms, not abstractive.
concepts: intuitive vs. abstractive knowledge of terms

gbs333-aaa394-d1e441.summary: Counter-objection: in an evident contingent proposition at least one term is an intuitive cognition, and if it were changed to an abstractive one it would no longer be the same term or proposition; so whoever has knowledge of the terms of such a proposition assents evidently, making it self-evident and a first principle.
claims: (Objection) Since the intuitive term is constitutive of the contingent proposition, it would be self-evident after all.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e463.summary: Solution: 'terms' here means not the mental signs composing the proposition but the things signified, which terminate acts of understanding and can be known intuitively or abstractively. A self-evident proposition must be evidently known whenever the signified things are apprehended, whether intuitively or abstractively. Cites Gregory of Rimini (I d. 2 q. 1 a. 1): being per se notum properly belongs not to the proposition but to the things signified, i.e., an enuntiabile is per se notum when knowledge of it depends on no extrinsic knowledge as its per se cause.
claims: 'Terms' in the definition of per se nota refers to the things signified, not the mental signs.
A proposition is self-evident only if it is evident however the signified things are apprehended, intuitively or abstractively.
(Gregory of Rimini) Self-evidence properly belongs to the signified enuntiabile, not to the proposition.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e522.summary: Infers that by 'terms' Ockham means either a concept existing objectively in the mind (on one opinion, cf. d. 3 q. 4) or the thing precisely signified by the extremes. Hence the proposition 'God is' formed by the blessed and that formed by us do not have the same terms; the former is self-evident and ours is not, since our terms do not signify God precisely, as we cannot know God under an absolute proper notion in this life.
claims: By 'terms' Ockham means objective concepts or the things precisely signified.
'God exists' as formed by the blessed is self-evident; as formed by us it is not.
We cannot know God by an absolute proper concept in this life.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e557.summary: Gives a briefer definition: a self-evident proposition is one for whose evidence its extremes, or any others signifying precisely the same, suffice. Refers to d. 3 q. 4, d'Ailly, and Ockham's sixth doubt.
claims: A self-evident proposition is one whose extremes, or any precisely equivalent ones, suffice for its evidence.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e576.summary: Third term, theological truth: a truth necessary for the wayfarer's salvation, i.e., one whose adhesive knowledge is necessary for salvation, explicitly or implicitly, for one with the use of reason who apprehends it. All truths in the biblical canon and those following necessarily from them are theological, but not all must be believed explicitly (e.g. that Abraham had two sons); it suffices to believe implicitly that everything revealed by God in the sense intended by the Holy Spirit is true, by which whatever follows from what is explicitly believed together with some truth is implicitly believed.
claims: A theological truth is one whose assent is necessary for salvation, explicitly or implicitly.
All truths in the biblical canon and their necessary consequences are theological truths.
Not all biblical truths must be believed explicitly; implicit belief in all revealed truths suffices.
Whatever follows from what is explicitly believed is implicitly believed.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e641.summary: This description of theological truth is strict; more broadly, any truth formed about God or about creatures as related to God (by governance, creation, conservation, justification, redemption) is called theological. Ockham relies on the first sense; d'Ailly holds the second more proper, citing an Augustine authority that Ockham also cites.
claims: Theological truth is taken strictly (necessary for salvation) or broadly (any truth about God or creatures as related to him).
Ockham uses the strict sense; d'Ailly prefers the broad.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e672.summary: Judges that d'Ailly cannot prove his point from the Augustine passage, which rather supports Ockham; but since the matter is agreed, disputing about the name is idle. D'Ailly's text is nonetheless useful for understanding Ockham.
claims: The Augustine passage supports Ockham's definition rather than d'Ailly's.
Once the substance is agreed, disputing about the name is pointless.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e688.summary: First consequence: some naturally known truths are theological, such as that God is good, living, wise, understanding, which Aristotle demonstrates in Metaphysics XII; such truths belong to both metaphysics and theology, being demonstrated quia in metaphysics and propter quid in theology.
claims: Some naturally known truths about God are theological truths.
Such truths belong to both metaphysics and theology.
They are demonstrated quia in metaphysics and propter quid in theology.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e710.summary: Second consequence: some theological truths are naturally known, others are known supernaturally and only believed by faith, such as that God is three and one, or that God is incarnate.
claims: Some theological truths are naturally knowable, others only believed by faith (Trinity, Incarnation).

gbs333-aaa394-d1e723.summary: Objection that the same truth would belong to different sciences. Reply: science is taken in two ways. First, aggregatively, for a collection of items pertaining to knowledge of one thing or of many with a determinate order: simple and complex apprehensive knowledge, assent to principles and conclusions, refutations of errors, solutions of fallacies, definitions and divisions (hence the definitive, divisive, and illative modes of procedure). So taken, many habits distinct in species and genus can be called one science by their special order, and one truth can belong to diverse sciences, even naturally discovered ones, and be a principle in one and a conclusion in another, as music's principles are proved in arithmetic.
claims: Science taken aggregatively is a collection of ordered cognitive items, including apprehensions, assents, refutations, definitions, and divisions.
Aggregate sciences have three modes of procedure: definitive, divisive, illative.
Many habits distinct in species can be one aggregate science by their special order.
In the aggregate sense the same truth can belong to different sciences and be a principle in one and a conclusion in another.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e796.summary: Second, science is taken for a simple quality or habit distinct from other intellectual habits; in this sense the same truth does not belong to distinct sciences, since one conclusion has only one science even if it can be demonstrated through diverse premises, and science so taken is numerically one thing.
claims: As a simple habit, science of one conclusion is one, even if demonstrable by different premises.
In this sense the same truth does not belong to distinct sciences.
concepts: unity of science of a conclusion

gbs333-aaa394-d1e816.summary: Distinguishes five senses of aggregate science: (1) generally, any collection of complex and incomplex, apprehensive and adhesive, actual and habitual cognitions ordered to knowing one or several things; (2) a collection of adhesive cognitions; (3) a collection of adhesive cognitions of necessary propositions, principles or conclusions; (4) a collection of cognitions of demonstrated conclusions only, actual and habitual; (5) a collection of habits of demonstrated conclusions only.
claims: Aggregate science has five progressively narrower senses.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e855.summary: The answer to whether natural philosophy (the knowledge in the Physics) is a science varies with these senses; in all of them 'science' functions as a collective noun, like 'army', which may denote only coordinated men, or men and animals, or all animals and equipment needed for battle, as with Holofernes' army in Judith 2.
claims: Whether a body of knowledge counts as 'a science' depends on the sense of aggregate science.
'Science' in the aggregate senses is a collective noun, like 'army'.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e892.summary: Applies the same distinction to habits: a habit taken aggregatively, containing many numerically and specifically distinct habits, cannot be both metaphysical and theological, so the habit by which one knows 'God is one' is in that sense neither, as a part is not the whole and a man is not an army; but taken as one simple habit, the same habit can be both metaphysical and theological, as a man can be part of an army or a people.
claims: Taken aggregatively, a habit cannot be both metaphysical and theological.
Taken as a simple habit, the same habit can belong to both metaphysics and theology.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e925.summary: Specifies that the question concerns evident knowledge in general, not precisely scientific evident knowledge.
claims: The question concerns evident knowledge generally, not only scientific knowledge.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e934.summary: Further specifies that the question concerns supernaturally knowable truths; for naturally knowable ones there is no difficulty, since they are obviously possible for the wayfarer.
claims: The question concerns supernaturally knowable theological truths.
Naturally knowable theological truths are evidently knowable by the wayfarer.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e951.summary: Begins the second article, on what knowledge of God a created intellect can have. Following d'Ailly, knowledge is sensory or intellectual (the former of little relevance), and each can be complex or incomplex, as brutes form many complex cognitions of sensibles. Refers to Gregory of Rimini d. 3.
claims: Knowledge is sensory or intellectual, and each may be complex or incomplex.
Brute animals form complex sensory cognitions.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e982.summary: Second notandum: incomplex knowledge possible to us is twofold, intuitive and abstractive (cf. Gerson, On the Magnificat, tract. 5).
claims: Incomplex knowledge is either intuitive or abstractive.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e995.summary: Defines intuitive knowledge: incomplex knowledge of a term or thing by virtue of which a contingent truth, especially about the present, can be evidently known, such as that the thing exists or not, or is here or there, as seeing Socrates makes evident that Socrates exists. If God conserved that vision after Socrates' destruction, one would evidently know by it that Socrates does not exist, which is possible only supernaturally, since intuition naturally depends causally on its object in becoming and being.
claims: Intuitive cognition is incomplex knowledge by which contingent truths about existence and presence can be evidently known.
If God conserved an intuition of a destroyed object, it would make evident that the object does not exist.
Naturally, intuitive cognition depends causally on its object.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e1030.summary: Intuitive knowledge extends not only to sensibles but to some intelligibles, namely our own acts (understanding, willing, delights, sorrows), not habits, since we evidently know that we understand, will, nill, and think. This holds when the intuition is sufficiently perfect; if too weak or obscure, or impeded by the object or medium, few contingent truths are evident. Experiential knowledge begins from intuition, and hence all intuitive knowledge is singular.
claims: We have intuitive knowledge of our own mental acts but not of our habits.
Weak or impeded intuitions may fail to yield evidence.
Experiential knowledge begins from intuitive knowledge.
All intuitive knowledge is singular.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e1076.summary: Abstractive knowledge is taken in two ways: (1) as universal knowledge abstracted from many singulars, such as the species concept of man; if universals are real qualities subjectively in the soul, such a universal can be intuitively seen, so the same knowledge can be intuitive and abstractive in this sense; (2) as knowledge abstracting from existence and non-existence and other contingent conditions, by which no contingent truth about the thing can be known, such as knowledge of an absent object. All naturally acquired abstractive knowledge of this second kind presupposes intuitive knowledge of the same object.
claims: Abstractive knowledge means either universal knowledge abstracted from singulars or knowledge abstracting from existence.
If universals are qualities in the soul, they can be intuitively known.
Abstractive knowledge (second sense) cannot ground contingent truths about existence.
Naturally acquired abstractive knowledge presupposes intuitive knowledge of the same object.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e1133.summary: Third notandum: the intellect has two acts, apprehensive and judicative. The apprehensive regards anything that can terminate a cognitive act, complex or incomplex (terms, propositions, arguments, syllogisms, demonstrations). The judicative is the act by which the intellect assents or dissents to a true or false proposition and concerns only propositional complexes. So regarding a proposition the intellect has two acts, and the first is separable from the second.
claims: The intellect has two kinds of act: apprehension and judgment.
Apprehension can concern anything intelligible; judgment concerns only propositions.
Apprehension of a proposition is separable from judgment about it.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e1176.summary: Others call the apprehensive act apprehensive knowledge and the judicative act adhesive knowledge. Apprehensive knowledge is the act by which we think of something complexly or incomplexly: incomplexly, as when one sees or hears the sky and thinks only of it; complexly-propositionally, as when one thinks that the heavens move; complexly non-propositionally, as when one thinks 'starry sky' or 'ploughed earth' without composing or dividing.
claims: Apprehensive knowledge may be incomplex, propositionally complex, or non-propositionally complex.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e1209.summary: Hence there can be apprehensive knowledge of any intelligible, whether thing outside or inside the soul, act, habit, science, or faith, though not every knowledge is apprehensive.
claims: Every intelligible can be the object of apprehensive knowledge.
Not every knowledge is apprehensive.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e1227.summary: Objection: of every intelligible there is apprehensive knowledge; every adhesive knowledge is intelligible; therefore every adhesive knowledge is apprehensive knowledge. Reply: a paralogism committing the fallacy of accident, since the minor extreme does not relate to the major in the conclusion as the middle does in the major; the correct conclusion is that of every adhesive knowledge there is apprehensive knowledge.
claims: The inference 'every adhesive knowledge is apprehensive knowledge' commits the fallacy of accident.
The valid conclusion is that every adhesive knowledge can be apprehended.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e1266.summary: Defines adhesive or judicative knowledge: the act by which the intellect assents or dissents to a propositional complex, believing it true or false; it concerns only propositional complexes.
claims: Adhesive knowledge is assent or dissent to a proposition and concerns only propositions.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e1279.summary: Interprets Ockham's claim that regarding a complex there are two acts. For spoken and written propositions it is plain: the corresponding mental proposition is the apprehensive act and assent to it the adhesive. For mental complexes it depends on the theory of concepts: if concepts have objective being, there are clearly two acts, apprehension and adhesion; if subjective being, a reflex act can take the mental proposition as object, and there can be several acts (the mental complex, its apprehension, and assent), though these are not always present, since we often assent to an external state of affairs without thinking of the mental proposition or the assent. Ockham's dictum is meant according to the fictum theory he explains in Prologue q. 7, on which the concept is not an act but something feigned by the act with objective being.
claims: For spoken and written propositions, the mental proposition is the apprehension and assent the adhesion.
On the fictum theory, a mental complex is the object of distinct acts of apprehension and adhesion.
On the act theory, reflex acts can make a mental proposition an object, but are not always present.
Ockham's statement is formulated according to the fictum theory.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e1388.summary: Fourth notandum: corresponding to the two acts there are two habits, apprehensive and judicative, each inclining immediately to its own act; no habit inclines to another habit's act except through its own act. The apprehensive habit inclines mediately to the adhesive act, since these habits are caused by those acts.
claims: There are apprehensive and judicative habits, each inclining immediately to its own act.
The apprehensive habit inclines to judgment only mediately.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e1415.summary: Transitional: preliminary conclusions to the responsive one are set out.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e1424.summary: First preambular proposition: the judicative act regarding a complex presupposes the apprehensive act of the same, i.e., adhesive knowledge presupposes apprehensive knowledge, understood intransitively as the mental proposition itself. Proof on the subjective-being theory: an act presupposes its object, and the apprehensive act is the immediate object of the adhesive act.
claims: Judgment presupposes apprehension of the same proposition.
On the act theory, the apprehensive act is the immediate object of assent.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e1453.summary: On the other (fictum) theory, where the object is a propositional complex with only objective being distinct from the apprehensive act, the conclusion still holds, since such a complex is an object only as apprehended; to be objectively in the intellect is just to be understood, so its apprehension is presupposed.
claims: On the fictum theory, too, assent presupposes apprehension, since objective being is just being understood.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e1477.summary: Second proposition, following from the first: judicative knowledge presupposes in the same power incomplex knowledge of the terms, since it presupposes knowledge of the complex and a whole presupposes its parts.
claims: Judgment presupposes incomplex knowledge of the terms in the same power.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e1495.summary: Third proposition: no act of a sensitive power is the immediate and proximate cause of an intellectual judgment. Ockham persuades rather than proves it, as it depends on a later principle: whatever object a lower power can attain, a higher power can attain under the same aspect. So whatever sense apprehends, the intellect apprehends too, and the incomplex knowledge of terms presupposed by judgment must be in the intellect.
claims: No sensory act is the immediate cause of an intellectual judgment.
Whatever a lower power can attain, a higher power can attain under the same aspect.
The intellect apprehends whatever the senses apprehend.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e1539.summary: Although the intellect assents to a contingent truth when its extremes are sensed and not when they are not, it does not follow that a sensory act is an immediate total or partial cause of intellectual judgment, though intellectual intuition cannot be had without sensation; sensation is a mediate cause, being the immediate cause of the first intellection.
claims: Sensation is a mediate, not immediate, cause of intellectual judgment.
Sensation is the immediate cause of the first intellection.
Intellectual intuition cannot naturally be had without sensory intuition.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e1564.summary: Sensation is required because intellectual intuition cannot be had without sensory intuition; nor is sensory intuition thereby superfluous, though intellectual intuition would suffice if it could be had without sensation, at least naturally, as in angels and separated souls.
claims: Sensory intuition is required for intellectual intuition in embodied humans.
Angels and separated souls have intellectual intuition without sensation.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e1586.summary: Fourth proposition: in this life our intellect can have two specifically distinct incomplex cognitions of the same object presented in the same way.
claims: The intellect can have two specifically distinct incomplex cognitions of one object.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e1597.summary: Fifth proposition: there are two incomplex cognitions, intuitive and abstractive.
claims: Incomplex knowledge is twofold: intuitive and abstractive.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e1608.summary: Sixth proposition: by his absolute power God can be known by both intuitive and abstractive cognition, each separable from the other.
claims: By God's absolute power, God can be known intuitively and abstractively, and the two cognitions are separable.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e1617.summary: Seventh proposition: abstractive knowledge of God is possible to the wayfarer, but intuitive knowledge is not, being repugnant to the wayfarer's state. Ockham and d'Ailly develop these propositions at length.
claims: Abstractive knowledge of God is possible in via.
Intuitive knowledge of God is incompatible with the wayfarer's state.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e1630.summary: Third article, Ockham's responsive conclusion: by his absolute power God can cause in a wayfarer's intellect evident knowledge of some theological truths, but not of others.
claims: By absolute power, God can cause in a wayfarer evident knowledge of some theological truths but not all.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e1653.summary: Two preliminaries. First, of things predicable of God, some are true extramental things and others concepts with only objective being (on one way of speaking); or, on another, some represent God distinctly in himself, wholly and in their parts, others represent God and creatures together. Second, theological truths are necessary or contingent ('God was', 'God is incarnate', 'God beatifies'), and of necessary ones some depend on contingent ones and some do not.
claims: Predicables of God are either things or concepts; or distinct or indistinct representations of God.
Theological truths are necessary or contingent.
Some necessary theological truths depend on contingent ones.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e1697.summary: Proves the conclusion: for some theological truths intuitive knowledge of a creature suffices for evidence, for others not; God can supply any creature's efficient causality; but the wayfarer cannot have intuitive knowledge of the deity, since that is beatific by common opinion. The following conclusions explain this first one.
claims: For some theological truths, intuitive knowledge of creatures suffices for evidence.
God can supply the efficient causality of any creature.
Intuitive knowledge of the deity is beatific and thus unavailable to the wayfarer.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e1723.summary: Second conclusion: God cannot cause in a wayfarer evident knowledge of a contingent theological truth whose evidence depends on intuitive knowledge of the deity, i.e., for which intuition of a creature does not suffice, such as 'the dead will rise', 'God beatifies souls perpetually', 'God will judge the living and the dead'. On 'God is man' Ockham answers ambiguously. Intuitive vision of God is repugnant to a creature in via.
claims: Contingent theological truths whose evidence requires intuition of God cannot be made evident to a wayfarer.
Examples include the resurrection, perpetual beatification, and the final judgment.
Ockham is ambiguous about whether 'God is man' can be made evident.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e1749.summary: Third conclusion: God cannot communicate to a wayfarer evident knowledge of necessary propositions with connotative predicates whose evidence depends on evident knowledge of a contingent proposition knowable only through intuition of the deity, such as perhaps 'God is incarnable'.
claims: Necessary connotative theological truths depending on contingent truths knowable only by intuition of God cannot be evident in via.
concepts: dependence of necessary on contingent truths

gbs333-aaa394-d1e1775.summary: Fourth conclusion: necessary theological truths in which a thing, a distinct cognition of the deity, or an absolute concept is predicated of God or of a distinct cognition of the deity are evidently knowable by such knowledge, e.g. 'God is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit', 'God is a being'. Their explanation depends on the next question and is omitted.
claims: Necessary theological truths with distinct cognitions or absolute concepts of God as terms are evidently knowable by that knowledge.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e1797.summary: Fourth article, first doubt: how Ockham can say that incomplex knowledge of terms, apprehension of a complex, and the following judgment are really distinct and separable by divine power. Biel explains that Ockham speaks according to the fictum theory, on which terms and complexes are objects rather than acts, and a mental complex is a simple object complex only representatively, as a word 'a' imposed to mean 'man is an animal' would be a simple quality yet signify complexly; Biel admits this is not his own view and he does not fully understand it. On his own view, apprehensive knowledge is just the act of understanding, called a concept (extended to syncategoremata), a natural likeness not in being but in representing, whose object is not a fictum but the extramental thing signified.
claims: Ockham's separability claim is framed according to the fictum theory.
On the fictum theory, a mental complex is a simple object that is complex only in representation.
Biel holds that a concept is the act of understanding itself, a natural likeness in representing.
The object of a concept is the extramental thing signified, not a fictum.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e1900.summary: Continues Biel's own view: as spoken and written propositions are composed of terms (subject, predicate, copula), so a mental proposition is really composed of distinct acts of understanding, really distinct qualities called concepts, corresponding to subject, predicate, and copula; the complex and its parts are apprehensive knowledge. Adhesive knowledge is another mental quality really distinct from them, whose immediate object is the apprehensive proposition: the soul tends by assent into the proposition, believing it true, and through it into the thing, believing it is as signified. This fits the common distinction of proximate and remote knowables.
claims: A mental proposition is really composed of distinct acts of understanding corresponding to subject, predicate, and copula.
Assent is a quality really distinct from the apprehensive proposition.
The immediate object of assent is the mental proposition; through it assent reaches the thing.
This grounds the distinction of proximate and remote objects of knowledge.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e1957.summary: On this view one sees how the cognitions are separable: prior ones from posterior, not conversely. Simple concepts are separable from the proposition as part from whole, and the proposition from judgment; but the proposition cannot be separated from its extremes, since a whole cannot exist without its parts.
claims: Concepts can exist without the proposition, and the proposition without judgment.
A proposition cannot exist without its constituent concepts.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e1977.summary: As for the judicative act, since it is a quality simply other than the apprehensive act and not part of it, Biel sees no reason why divine power could not separate it from the apprehension (the proposition); though apprehension is an essential cause of judgment, it is an extrinsic cause, whose causality God can supply, producing or conserving the judgment with the apprehension destroyed.
claims: God can conserve an act of assent without the corresponding apprehension.
Apprehension is an extrinsic cause of judgment whose causality God can supply.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e2003.summary: Objection: it is contradictory for there to be assent without that to which one assents: 'I have assent, so I assent to something'; if there is no apprehension, there is nothing assented to, so one would assent to something and to nothing.
claims: (Objection) Assent without an apprehended object is contradictory.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e2025.summary: Reply: the quality that is really the judicative act can be conserved by God in the intellect without the intellect's tending through it to an object, so 'I have assent (that quality), therefore I assent to something' does not follow.
claims: The quality that is assent can exist without the intellect being directed through it to an object.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e2043.summary: Further objection: assent is defined as a mental quality by which one tends, believing, into a truth or apparent truth; so by inference from definitum to definition, having assent entails tending into something true to which one assents.
claims: (Objection) By definition, having assent entails tending into a true object.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e2057.summary: Reply: 'assent' can be taken absolutely, signifying the quality without connotation, or connotatively, signifying the quality while connoting its tending into a true object. Taken absolutely, 'I have assent, so I assent to something' does not follow; taken connotatively, it does, but then when the tendency is destroyed and the quality preserved, the quality remains without being called assent, since the connotatum is lacking. So assent can still be separated from apprehension, though it no longer bears the name, just as a two-foot body condensed to one foot remains the same thing but loses the name 'two-foot'.
claims: 'Assent' can be taken absolutely (the quality) or connotatively (the quality as directed to a truth).
The quality of assent can persist without its connotatum, losing the name 'assent'.
Assent is thus separable from apprehension in reality though not under its connotative name.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e2105.summary: Second doubt: how to understand Ockham's saying (here, d. 2 q. 7, Prologue q. 2) that things are predicated and subjected, distinguishing thing from sign and from objective concepts; why he multiplies expressions like 'from knowledge of the thing or things, or the terms'; and his claim (Prologue q. 2) that 'God exists' as we have it is not self-evident while that formed by the blessed is, because the blessed predicate the essence of the essence in itself, whereas in our proposition a concept is predicated. What then is meant by 'term', 'thing', or 'sign' as distinguished from thing?
claims: (Doubt) Ockham's talk of things being subjects and predicates needs explanation.
(Ockham) 'God exists' as formed by the blessed is self-evident, unlike ours.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e2170.summary: Biel answers as he understands it, noting he does not accept that being subject, predicate, or term belongs to a thing except significatively, and that Ockham himself departs from that way of speaking in Book I and in the Quodlibets. He quotes Ockham's self-exposition in Prologue q. 2: talk of a thing being predicated in divinis is according to the opinion that the intellection is not the subject or predicate but its object, which Ockham considers probable; according to the other, also probable, opinion that every subject of a mental proposition is an intellection or quality in the mind, the proposition the blessed form about God is composed not of the thing but of a distinct intention.
claims: Biel holds that things are subjects or predicates only significatively.
Ockham's 'thing is predicated' language follows the fictum opinion; on the act opinion, the blessed's proposition is composed of a distinct intention, not of God himself.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e2214.summary: From that statement it seems that, on the first opinion, being subject, predicate, or term is attributed to a thing really, not just in objective being: in Prologue q. 9 Ockham says the subject is that for which there is supposition, some singular, taking 'subject' and 'predicate' participially. The division in this question's fifth article (some predicables of God are true extramental things, others only concepts with objective being) and Prologue q. 2 reflect that opinion, which Ockham commonly follows in Book I and according to which many of his statements must be understood.
claims: On one opinion Ockham attributes being subject and predicate to things themselves, really or objectively.
'Subject' and 'predicate' are then taken participially, for what is supposited for.
Many of Ockham's Book I statements presuppose that opinion.
concepts: participial vs. nominal sense of subject

gbs333-aaa394-d1e2284.summary: On the other opinion, which Ockham also holds probable and eventually adopts, abandoning the first, being subject, predicate, term, complex or incomplex belongs to signs. Biel judges that Ockham often uses both ways of speaking, conforming to those whose views he reports: by 'thing' predicated or subjected he means a distinct concept of the thing, by 'concept' an indistinct concept. As we cannot see God intuitively in via, neither can we have a distinct concept of God, unlike the blessed, who seeing God face to face form other propositions with other terms, since what terminates their cognition is God clearly seen and their concept is a clear cognition of God (cf. d. 3 q. 4).
claims: Ockham ultimately adopts the view that being subject, predicate, and term belongs to signs.
When Ockham says a 'thing' is predicated, he means a distinct concept of it.
Wayfarers lack distinct concepts of God; the blessed have them through face-to-face vision.
The blessed form different propositions about God, with different terms, from wayfarers.
concepts: development of Ockham's theory of concepts

gbs333-aaa394-d1e2343.summary: Thus Ockham's claim in Prologue q. 2 (we cannot have that proposition nor its terms, since in ours a concept is predicated and in theirs the divine essence in itself) means: the extremes of our mental proposition are common concepts, those of the blessed distinct concepts; and the 'terms', i.e., the things terminating the cognitions, also differ, since the blessed clearly see God and the wayfarer does not. Objects terminating cognitions are called terms.
claims: Our propositions about God have common concepts as extremes; the blessed's have distinct concepts.
The objects terminating cognitions are called 'terms' and differ between wayfarer and blessed.
concepts: common vs. distinct concepts of God

gbs333-aaa394-d1e2388.summary: Adds that, as Prologue q. 2 shows, in this life we can have distinct knowledge of almost nothing unsensed, and forming a concept of a thing in itself requires its presence moving the intellect as object; hence instead of 'distinct concept' Ockham often says the thing itself is predicated or subjected, because the thing is a partial cause of the distinct concept. So the blessed form different propositions with different terms than we do. Similarly with creatures: propositions about something known intuitively vs. abstractively, or sensed vs. unsensed, are different propositions with different terms. Ockham also seems to hold that the external senses know corporeal substance not in itself (d. 3 q. 2), so his statements often need moderating. Thus there are two ways of speaking: being subject and predicate belongs to things (really or objectively) or to signs; and a thing is said to be subjected 'in itself' because a distinct cognition of it is subject or predicate.
claims: We can have distinct knowledge only of sensed things, with few exceptions.
A thing is a partial cause of its distinct concept, which is why Ockham speaks of the thing as predicated.
Propositions from intuitive vs. abstractive cognition of the same thing have different terms.
(Ockham) No external corporeal substance can be naturally known by us in itself.
Two ways of speaking: subject and predicate belong to things, or to signs.
concepts: object as partial cause of concept

gbs333-aaa394-d1e2486.summary: To the question what the act of understanding terminates at, refers to Prologue q. 7, d. 2 q. 8, and d. 3 q. 4 (and the corresponding place in the Collectorium).

gbs333-aaa394-d1e2508.summary: Explains the terminology according to each opinion. External things are called 'terms' because they are objects of terms (concepts in objective being) or because they terminate cognition mediately or immediately. On the fictum opinion, 'complex' and 'incomplex' name not cognitions but their immediate objects, so Ockham speaks of 'knowledge of a complex' transitively, and takes 'concept' participially for the immediate object of conception. On that view, the intellect seeing an external thing feigns in itself a likeness having objective being corresponding to the thing's subjective being (d. 2 q. 8), which is the immediate object of the act. There are thus two objects: the ultimate, moving object, presupposed by the act and its partial cause (per Augustine, knowledge is born of knower and known), and the immediately terminating object, a medium through which the intellect tends to the thing, which does not move the intellect but is constituted in objective being by the act and follows it by nature, since its being is just being understood. This fictum supposits for the thing because of its representative likeness.
claims: External things are 'terms' as objects of concepts or as terminating cognition.
On the fictum theory, 'complex' and 'incomplex' denote objects of cognition, not cognitions.
The fictum is a likeness feigned by the intellect, with objective being corresponding to the thing's real being.
On that theory there is an ultimate moving object (partial cause of cognition) and an immediate terminating object (the fictum).
The fictum's being is its being understood; it supposits for the thing it resembles.
concepts: Augustine on the genesis of knowledge

gbs333-aaa394-d1e2636.summary: Others, denying ficta, say the intellect is directly borne into the thing, taking 'concept' not participially as object of cognition but nominally for the real quality in the soul, and 'complex' and 'incomplex' for the complex or incomplex act of understanding. Ockham often frames questions according to the fictum view (e.g. whether the first thing known is a universal), which others phrase as whether the first cognition is universal. Since Ockham considers both opinions probable, he doubles his terms to satisfy both; the prudent reader should decide what to say according to the opinion he embraces and interpret Ockham accordingly.
claims: Opponents of ficta hold that the intellect is borne directly into things.
On that view, concepts and complexes are real mental qualities (acts).
Ockham doubles his terminology to accommodate both probable opinions.
The reader should interpret Ockham according to the opinion he adopts.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e2691.summary: Supports this reading from Ockham's solution to the sixth doubt (in his Scriptum): intuitive knowledge and the subsequent judgment are really distinct because intuitive knowledge concerns the incomplex and judgment the complex, which holds if concepts have objective being and complex and incomplex are objects rather than mental acts; on the other opinion one would say intuitive knowledge is incomplex knowledge.
claims: Ockham's claim that intuition and judgment are really distinct is framed on the fictum theory.
On the act theory, intuitive knowledge is described as incomplex knowledge.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e2724.summary: Further evidence that by 'terms' Ockham means things: in the next question's third article he says one who distinctly understood the divine essence and predicated it of itself could not doubt the proposition, which would be known from the terms, i.e., from the things terminating the cognition; and that the middle of demonstration is either the thing or its concept, 'thing' meaning a distinct concept according to some, otherwise on the other opinion.
claims: Ockham uses 'terms' for the things terminating cognition.
'Thing' as middle term means a distinct concept according to some interpreters.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e2758.summary: Third doubt, against the claim that the same knowledge can be intuitive and abstractive: abstractive knowledge (in the relevant sense) is universal and intuitive knowledge singular; and no knowledge is its own object, else act and object would coincide. Reply: Ockham only means that a universal with real being in the soul can be intuitively known, on the opinion that concepts have subjective being. I can evidently know that I assent to 'every man is an animal' and so that I have common concepts of man and animal, moved by that universal concept as object; but the universal cognition is not formally intuitive of itself. It is intuitive by subordination, since concepts are subordinated to concepts as words to concepts (as the concept of the word 'man' is subordinated to the specific concept man). So the universal concept is formally abstractive and intuitive by subordination to the singular knowledge that is its natural likeness: the same knowledge is intuitive and abstractive, but equivocally.
claims: A universal existing really in the soul can be intuitively known.
We can know evidently that we assent to propositions and possess common concepts.
Concepts can be subordinated to other concepts as words are to concepts.
A universal concept is abstractive formally and intuitive only by subordination; the same knowledge is intuitive and abstractive only equivocally.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e2852.summary: On the other objection (that no knowledge is its own object): as noted earlier, the intellect knows its acts by reflex cognition broadly taken, and there is a stopping point at the first reflex cognition, as Ockham argues in his fourth doubt. In this life that intellection impedes a second intuition, not absolutely, but because the principal first reflex intellection does not suffice for a second, whose cause may be the nature of the thing, since we experience such impediment in ourselves.
claims: The intellect knows its own acts by reflex cognition.
Reflection stops at the first reflex cognition.
In this life a further reflex intuition is impeded, as experience shows.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e2889.summary: Fourth doubt: since Ockham says nothing is known intuitively that is not also known abstractively under the same aspect, are intuitive and abstractive knowledge of the same object synonymous? It seems so: synonymous cognitions signify precisely the same in the same way, and intuitive and abstractive cognition of one object do so, otherwise something would be known intuitively under an aspect not abstractively knowable, contrary to Ockham.
claims: (Argument) Intuitive and abstractive cognitions of the same object seem synonymous, since they signify the same under the same aspect.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e2935.summary: Anticipates the reply that intuition knows a thing's existence and abstraction does not: existence is also known abstractively, since one can conceive an object as existing while doubting whether it exists, which is not intuitive; and intuition can be of a non-existent, as Ockham proves.
claims: Existence can be conceived abstractively while doubted.
Intuition can be of a non-existent object.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e2959.summary: Argument against synonymy: synonymous cognitions differ only in number and represent the object the same way with the same effects; but intuitive and abstractive differ in species and intuitive causes evident knowledge of existence while abstractive cannot. Biel nevertheless judges, without prejudice to better views, that they are synonymous. Synonymous cognitions need not be of the same species, as with a word and its concept, or subordinated concepts, which differ in species yet are synonymous; nor must synonymous cognitions cause the same cognitions, but only have the same object under precisely the same aspect, i.e., signify the same in the same way. Ockham shows sufficiently whence their specific difference arises if not from their mode of signifying.
claims: (Objection) Intuitive and abstractive cognitions differ in species and effects, so are not synonymous.
Biel holds intuitive and abstractive cognitions of the same object are synonymous.
Synonymous signs need not be of the same species (e.g. word and concept).
Synonymy requires only the same object under the same aspect, not the same causal effects.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e3024.summary: Fifth doubt, on supernaturally conserved or produced intuitive knowledge of a non-existent: can it make evident that the thing does not exist when it does not? Ockham often says so but does not prove it, and it is not known by experience. Proof proposed: let a be a perfect intuition of a non-existent produced or conserved by God; by it some contingent truth about its object must be evidently knowable, else it would be abstractive; not that the object exists, which is false and cannot be known; therefore that the object does not exist.
claims: (Argument) A supernaturally conserved intuition of a non-existent makes evident that the object does not exist, since it must ground some contingent truth and cannot ground a false one.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e3067.summary: Possible reply: it suffices for intuitive knowledge that it can cause evidence of a contingent proposition predicating existence of its object in the common course of nature; its persisting after its object's corruption is supernatural.
claims: (Reply) Intuition need only cause evident knowledge of existence in the ordinary course of nature.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e3083.summary: Rebuttal: supernatural production or conservation of intuitive knowledge does not remove its natural action or power, as an eye supernaturally given to one born blind would see naturally, and eucharistic accidents conserved without subject still heat, cool, and cause sensations. So intuition supernaturally conserved without its object retains its natural operation of causing evident knowledge that its object exists or does not exist.
claims: Supernatural conservation does not remove a thing's natural powers.
Eucharistic accidents without a subject retain their natural actions.
A supernaturally conserved intuition can still naturally cause evident knowledge of its object's existence or non-existence.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e3129.summary: Further argument: God can infuse knowledge by which I evidently know Antichrist does not exist; by definition it is intuitive, yet it is of a non-existent.
claims: God can infuse intuitive knowledge evidently showing that something (e.g. Antichrist) does not exist.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e3142.summary: Further argument: God can infuse and conserve incomplex knowledge of a singular by which I can evidently know every disposition of it however it changes, causing evident knowledge that it exists when it does and does not when it does not. Those who hold that angels know by concreated species must say something similar: either Gabriel has one species of Peter by which he knows all Peter's states, including that Peter is a man and later is not, so one cognition suffices (since acts vary only with species on their view); or he has a concreated species for each state, but since infinitely many variations are possible, he would have infinitely many concreated species of Peter, which is absurd.
claims: God can infuse a single knowledge of a singular that tracks all its changes, including its non-existence.
Defenders of angelic concreated species must accept a single species representing all states of an object.
Positing a distinct concreated species for every state would require infinitely many species, which is absurd.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e3203.summary: Further argument from Scotus: the same intuitive cognition by which one knows the Word and creatures in the Word does not vary with creatures' variation, so by it one knows a thing exists when it does and does not when it does not.
claims: (Scotus) The beatific cognition of creatures in the Word is invariant and reveals both their existence and non-existence.

gbs333-aaa394-d1e3219.summary: Final argument: God by one eternal, immutable act intuitively knows everything existent and non-existent, that things are when they are and are not when corrupted; this does not seem impossible in creatures, since knowing and understanding belong univocally and properly to God and creatures. These reasons, though not demonstrative, are very persuasive.
claims: God knows by one immutable intuitive act both the existence and non-existence of things.
Knowing and understanding are univocal between God and creatures.
The arguments for evident intuitive knowledge of non-existence are persuasive though not demonstrative.

gbs333-aaa394.summary: Quaestio 1, the foundational question of the prologue, asks whether a wayfarer's intellect can have evident knowledge of theological truths. Article 1 defines the terms. A wayfarer lacks intuitive vision of God permanently possible to him by ordained power, which addresses the cases of Christ and Paul's rapture against d'Ailly. Evident knowledge is assent apt to be caused by knowledge of the terms or of other propositions, cuts across necessity, and is broader than science; self-evidence is relative to the things signified, so 'God exists' is self-evident to the blessed but not to us. A theological truth is one necessary for salvation, explicitly or implicitly, so some are naturally knowable and shared with metaphysics while others are only believed, and the notion of aggregate science, a collective term like 'army', explains how one truth belongs to several sciences. Article 2 sets out Ockham's cognitive psychology. Intuitive cognition grounds evident contingent judgments about existence, including of our own acts, and could make non-existence evident by divine power. Abstractive cognition abstracts from existence and presupposes intuition. Apprehension and judgment are distinct acts, with judgment presupposing apprehension and knowledge of terms, and sensation only a mediate cause of intellectual judgment. God can be known intuitively and abstractively, but only abstractively in via. Article 3 concludes that by absolute power God can cause evident knowledge of some theological truths in a wayfarer, namely those for which intuition of creatures suffices, but not of contingent truths like the resurrection and judgment, or the necessary truths depending on them, that require intuitive vision of God. Article 4's doubts develop Biel's interpretation of Ockham's two theories of concepts (fictum and act). Biel himself holds the act theory and argues that God could conserve assent without apprehension. He explains Ockham's talk of things as predicates as shorthand for distinct concepts, and treats the intuition of universals by subordination. He judges, against appearances, that intuitive and abstractive cognitions of one object are synonymous, and gives persuasive though not demonstrative arguments that a supernaturally conserved intuition makes evident the non-existence of its object.
claims: By absolute power God can cause evident knowledge of some, but not all, theological truths in a wayfarer.
Contingent theological truths whose evidence requires intuitive vision of God, and necessary truths depending on them, cannot be made evident to a wayfarer.
Intuitive cognition grounds evident judgments of contingent existence; abstractive cognition does not and naturally presupposes intuition.
In via God can be known abstractively but not intuitively; we have no distinct concept of God.
Apprehension and judgment are really distinct acts; judgment presupposes apprehension, though God could conserve the quality of assent without it.
A theological truth is one whose assent is necessary for salvation explicitly or implicitly; some theological truths are also metaphysical.
Biel holds the act theory of concepts while explaining Ockham's statements made according to the fictum theory.
concepts: fictum vs. intellectio theory of concepts
distinct vs. common concepts of God
